q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE cause of increased interregional trade in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the Mongol Empire facilitated trade, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which increased trade affected societies along the trade routes in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450.

sample_answers.a: The Mongol conquests created a relatively secure overland corridor across Eurasia (the Pax Mongolica), lowering the risks and costs of caravan trade between China, Central Asia, and Europe.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the Mongols protected merchants, maintained relay stations, and enforced a single legal order across their vast territory, so traders could travel from China to the Black Sea under one imperial peace.
sample_answers.c: Trade spread not only goods but also technologies (such as gunpowder and printing), religions (Islam and Buddhism along the routes), and diseases (including the bubonic plague that devastated Eurasia in the 1340s).

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the surge of interregional trade between 1200 and 1450 as the result of empire, technology, and demand reinforcing each other. The Mongol conquests, for all their destruction, created the largest contiguous empire in history and with it a zone of relative security — the Pax Mongolica — in which merchants, missionaries, and diplomats could travel from China to Europe. Maritime technology advanced in parallel: the magnetic compass, the sternpost rudder, and larger ships like Chinese junks and Arab dhows made the Indian Ocean and South China Sea into highways of commerce. Underlying it all was demand: the wealthy elites of Song China, the Islamic world, and Europe craved each other's luxuries — silk, spices, porcelain, horses — and merchants organized ever more ambitious networks to supply them.
—Historian's account of interregional trade in the period c. 1200–1450

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of the port city described by Ibn Battuta.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Ibn Battuta's account shows the scale of Indian Ocean trade.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan scholar, was able to travel so widely across the Islamic world and beyond.

sample_answers.a: Ibn Battuta describes a great harbor crowded with large ships from China, Arabia, and India, with merchants of many nations trading in its markets.
sample_answers.b: The presence of Chinese junks, Arab dhows, and Indian vessels in a single port — carrying porcelain, spices, textiles, and horses — shows a maritime network linking East Asia, South Asia, and the Middle East.
sample_answers.c: The shared Islamic faith gave him lodging, legal standing, and employment (as a judge) across Muslim lands, while the Mongol peace and established trade routes made long-distance travel practical and relatively safe.

q2.stimulus:
We came to the great harbor, one of the largest in the world, crowded with ships from China, Arabia, and Persia. The merchants are wealthy and the markets overflow with goods: Chinese porcelain and silk, Indian pepper and textiles, Arabian horses and pearls. Vessels of enormous size lie at anchor, their holds filled with cargoes for distant ports. In the warehouses along the shore, goods are stored that will travel to Cairo, to Samarkand, to the lands of the Franks. Never have I seen a port where the commerce of so many nations meets in one place.
—Adapted from Ibn Battuta, The Rihla (Travels), c. 1355

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of Zheng He's voyages shown on the map.
parts.b: Explain ONE purpose of Zheng He's expeditions beyond trade.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why China ended the voyages after the 1430s despite their success.

sample_answers.a: The map shows Zheng He's fleets sailing from Nanjing across the South China Sea, through Southeast Asia, across the Indian Ocean to India, Arabia, and East Africa — voyages far longer than any contemporary European expedition.
sample_answers.b: The expeditions were instruments of Ming diplomacy and prestige: the treasure ships awed foreign rulers, collected tribute, and demonstrated China's wealth and power, extending the tribute system across the Indian Ocean.
sample_answers.c: The voyages were enormously expensive, Confucian officials opposed their extravagance, and the Ming court turned inward to face Mongol threats on the northern frontier — so the state redirected resources from maritime expansion to land defense.

q3.stimulus: The image is a page from the Mao Kun map (published in the Ming military treatise Wubei Zhi, 1621, based on Zheng He's navigation charts), showing the voyager routes from Nanjing through Southeast Asia, across the Indian Ocean, and to the Persian Gulf and East Africa. The map documents the seven great expeditions of Admiral Zheng He (1405–1433), whose treasure fleets — with ships far larger than any in Europe — carried Chinese porcelain, silk, and diplomacy across the known maritime world.
